name: Soares nose shaper (1905)

lead: The Soares nose shaper is an early-1900s patented appliance for reshaping the nose without surgery. The inventor, of Framingham, Massachusetts, described a bendable metal body with a soft lining that grips the nose sides, plus a tongue under the tip, held on with tapes.
It was intended for upturned, one-sided, flat or wide-nostril noses, giving slow, steady pressure over time. It belongs to a family of mechanical nose shapers of the era; no results data are known.

paras: The patent describes bending the device to the desired nose shape and wearing it with tapes that cross behind the neck and buckle over the forehead, recommended at night. One side could be bent more for a one-sided nose.

The patent claims painless correction. A historical commentary on a similar 1894 device by an author who tried it reported sleep disturbance and facial injuries from sharp metal, and he doubted lasting results.

lead: The Soares nose shaper is described in US Patent 850,978, 'Nose-shaper', filed on 12 October 1905 by Ignatius Nathaniel Soares of Framingham, Massachusetts, and granted on 23 April 1907. [1]

The patent says the device is meant to correct upturned, one-sided, flat or distended-nostril noses with gentle but continuous pressure. [1] A body of tempered sheet metal can be bent to the desired shape, lined with chamois or fabric, with a tongue that presses on the underside and bands that hold it on. [1]

It was one of several mechanical nose-shaping appliances of the period; the German Zello-Punkt, patented in 1894, was a brass version worn overnight. [2] No studies or records of results from the Soares device are known.
infobox: Tempered sheet metal, chamois or fabric lining [1]

paras: The patent specifies a body portion of resilient material, best thin tempered sheet metal, which can be bent and holds its shape. A soft lining of chamois or fabric prevents skin irritation and improves grip, and a tongue rests under the nose and can press up on the cartilage between the nostrils. [1]

The device is bent to the nose shape desired, and bands go behind the neck, cross, and buckle across the forehead, producing slight steady tension. The inventor recommends night wear. For a one-sided nose, one side is bent more, or the bands are shifted to press more on that side. [1]

The Zello-Punkt Model 21 (1894) was a brass appliance with screws, a leather cushion and a rubber band, sold through hairdressers and pharmacies and used at night for months. [2] Its commentator doubts it achieved cosmetic results and reports discomfort when he tried it. [2] Modern surgeons quoted about today's nose clips state that such devices do not remodel adult cartilage. [3]
